units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS
May I do it?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: No.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Gravely .
You are wrong, Lady Chiltern.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: No. The letter must be intercepted. That is all. But how can I do it? Letters arrive for him every moment of the day. His secretaries open them and hand them to him. I dare not ask the servants to bring me his letters. It would be impossible. Oh! why don’t you tell me what to do?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Pray be calm, Lady Chiltern, and answer the questions I am going to put to you. You said his secretaries open his letters.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Yes.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Who is with him to-day? Mr. Trafford, isn’t it?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: No. Mr. Montford, I think.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: You can trust him?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: With a gesture of despair .
Oh! how do I know?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: He would do what you asked him, wouldn’t he?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I think so.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Your letter was on pink paper. He could recognise it without reading it, couldn’t he? By the colour?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I suppose so.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Is he in the house now?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Yes.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Then I will go and see him myself, and tell him that a certain letter, written on pink paper, is to be forwarded to Robert to-day, and that at all costs it must not reach him.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Goes to the door , and opens it .
Oh! Robert is coming upstairs with the letter in his hand. It has reached him already.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: With a cry of pain .
Oh! you have saved his life; what have you done with mine?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Enter SIR ROBERT CHILTERN.
He has the letter in his hand , and is reading it .
He comes towards his wife , not noticing LORD GORING’S presence .

‘I want you. I trust you. I am coming to you. Gertrude.’ Oh, my love! Is this true? Do you indeed trust me, and want me? If so, it was for me to come to you, not for you to write of coming to me. This letter of yours, Gertrude, makes me feel that nothing that the world may do can hurt me now. You want me, Gertrude?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: LORD GORING, unseen by SIR ROBERT CHILTERN, makes an imploring sign to LADY CHILTERN to accept the situation and SIR ROBERT’S error .
Yes.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: You trust me, Gertrude?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Yes.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Ah! why did you not add you loved me?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Taking his hand .
Because I loved you.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: LORD GORING passes into the conservatory .
Kisses her .

Gertrude, you don’t know what I feel. When Montford passed me your letter across the table—he had opened it by mistake, I suppose, without looking at the handwriting on the envelope—and I read it—oh! I did not care what disgrace or punishment was in store for me, I only thought you loved me still.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: There is no disgrace in store for you, nor any public shame. Mrs. Cheveley has handed over to Lord Goring the document that was in her possession, and he has destroyed it.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Are you sure of this, Gertrude?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Yes; Lord Goring has just told me.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Then I am safe! Oh! what a wonderful thing to be safe! For two days I have been in terror. I am safe now. How did Arthur destroy my letter? Tell me.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: He burned it.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: I wish I had seen that one sin of my youth burning to ashes. How many men there are in modern life who would like to see their past burning to white ashes before them! Is Arthur still here?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Yes; he is in the conservatory.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: I am so glad now I made that speech last night in the House, so glad. I made it thinking that public disgrace might be the result. But it has not been so.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Public honour has been the result.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: I think so. I fear so, almost. For although I am safe from detection, although every proof against me is destroyed, I suppose, Gertrude . . . I suppose I should retire from public life?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN
